units.name: Understanding the User: Individual goals and interactions with others

topics-cs.description: User-centered design and evaluation methods. (See also: SEP-Context, SEP-Ethical-Analysis, SEP-Professional-Ethics)

topics.description: User stories/storytelling and techniques for gathering stories
Needs assessment (techniques for uncovering needs and gathering requirements - e.g., interviews, surveys, ethnographic and contextual enquiry) (See also: SE-Requirements)
Interfacing with stakeholders, as a team
Risks associated with physical, distributed, hybrid and virtual teams

topics-ka.description: Physical and cognitive characteristics of the user

topics.description: Physical capabilities that inform interaction design (e.g., color perception, ergonomics)
Cognitive models that inform interaction design (e.g., attention, perception and recognition, movement, memory)
Topics in social/behavioral psychology (e.g., cognitive biases, change blindness)

topics-ka.description: Designing for diverse user populations. (See also: SEP-DEIA, HCI-Accessibility)

topics.description: How differences (e.g., in race, ability, age, gender, culture, experience, and education) impact user experiences and needs
Designing for users from other cultures
Challenges to effective design evaluation. (e.g., sampling, generalization; disability and disabled experiences)

topics-ka.description: Collaboration and communication (See also: AI-SEP, SE-Teamwork, SEP-Communication, SPD-Game)

topics.description: Understanding the user in a multi-user context
Synchronous group communication (e.g., chat rooms, conferencing, online games)
Asynchronous group communication (e.g., email, forums, social networks)
Social media, social computing, and social network analysis

outcomes-cs.description: Conduct a user-centered design process that is integrated into a project.

outcomes-ka.description: Compare and contrast the needs of users with those of designers.
Identify the representative users of a design and discuss who else could be impacted by it.
Describe empathy and evaluation as elements of the design process.
Carry out and document an analysis of users and their needs.
Construct a user story from a needs assessment.
Redesign an existing solution to a population whose needs differ from those of the initial target population.
Contrast the different needs-finding methods for a given design problem.
Reflect on whether your design would benefit from low-tech or no-tech components.

outcomes-non.description: Recognize the implications of designing for a multi-user system/context.

topics.description: Safety, security and privacy (See also: SEP-Security, SEC-Foundations)
Harm and disparate impact (See also: SEP-DEIA)

topics-cs.description: Ethics in design methods and solutions (See also: SEP-Ethical-Analysis, SEP-Context, SEP-Intellectual Property)

topics.description: The role of artificial intelligence (See also: AI-SEP)
Responsibilities for considering stakeholder impact and human factors (See also: SEP-Professional-Ethics)
Role of design to meet user needs
Consideration beyond immediate user needs, including via iterative reconstruction of problem analysis and “digital well-being” features

topics-ka.description: Value-sensitive design (See also: SEP-Ethical-Analysis, SEP-Context, SEP-Communication)

topics.description: Determine and include diverse stakeholder values and value systems.
Assess the persuasive content of a design
Employ persuasion as a design goal
Distinguish persuasive interfaces from manipulative interfaces

outcomes-cs.description: Identify and critique the potential impacts of a design on society and relevant communities to address such concerns as sustainability, inclusivity, safety, security, privacy, harm, and disparate impact.

outcomes-ka.description: Identify the potential human factor elements in a design.
Identify and understand direct and indirect stakeholders.
Develop scenarios that consider the entire lifespan of a design, beyond the immediately planned uses that anticipate direct and indirect stakeholders.

Identify and critique the potential factors in a design that impact direct and indirect stakeholders and broader society (e.g., transparency, sustainability of the system, trust, artificial intelligence).
Assess the persuasive content of a design and its intent relative to user interests.
Critique the outcomes of a design given its intent.
Understand the impact of design decisions.

topics.description: Societal and legal support for and obligations to people with disabilities
Accessibility standards (e.g., Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) (See also: SPD-Web)
Features and products that enable accessibility and support inclusive development by designers and engineers
Demographics and populations (permanent, temporary, and situational disability)
International perspectives on disability (See also: SEP-DEIA)
Attitudes towards people with disabilities (See also: SEP-DEIA)
Software engineering practices that enable inclusion and accessibility. (See also: SEP-DEIA)
Examples of accessibility-enabling features, such as conformance to screen readers
Creating inclusive processes such as participatory design

topics-non.description: Technologies: the Return On Investment (ROI) of inclusion
Inclusive Design Frameworks: user-sensitive inclusive design (See also: SEP-DEIA)
Critical approaches to HCI (e.g., inclusivity) (See also: SEP-DEIA)

outcomes-cs.description: Identify accessibility challenges faced by people with different disabilities and specify the associated accessible and assistive technologies that address them. (See also: AI-Agents, AI-Robotics)
Identify appropriate inclusive design approaches, such as universal design and ability-based design.
Identify and demonstrate understanding of software accessibility guidelines.
Demonstrate recognition of laws and regulations applicable to accessible design.

outcomes-ka.description: Apply inclusive frameworks to design, such as universal design and usability and ability-based design, and demonstrate accessible design of visual, voice-based, and touch-based UIs.
Demonstrate understanding of laws and regulations applicable to accessible design.
Demonstrate understanding of what is appropriate and inappropriate high level of skill during interaction with individuals from diverse populations.
Analyze web pages and mobile apps for current standards of accessibility.

outcomes-non.description: Biases towards disability, race, and gender have historically, either intentionally or unintentionally, informed technology design.

topics.description: Consider how those experiences (learnings?) might inform design.

outcomes-non.description: Conceptualize user experience research to identify user needs and generate design insights.

topics.description: Formative (e.g., needs-finding, exploratory analysis) and summative assessment (e.g., functionality and usability testing)
Elements to evaluate (e.g., utility, efficiency, learnability, user satisfaction, affective elements such as pleasure and engagement)
Understanding ethical approval requirements before engaging in user research (See also: SE-Tools, SEP-Ethical-Analysis, SEP-Security, SEP-Privacy, SEP-Professional-Ethics)

topics-ka.description: Methods for evaluation with users (See also: SE-Validation)

topics.description: Qualitative methods (qualitative coding and thematic analysis)
Mixed methods (e.g., observation, think-aloud, interview, survey, experiment)
Challenges and shortcomings to effective evaluation (e.g., sampling, generalization)
Approvals from Institutional Research Boards and ethics committees (See also: SEP-Ethical-Analysis, SEP-Security, SEP-Privacy)

Evaluate the implications and broader impacts of a given design.

Conduct a usability evaluation of a given user interface and draw defensible conclusions given the study design.

Pre-register a study design, with planned statistical tests.
